08.01.title: The harmonic oscillator
08.01.html:
Pluck a guitar string, tap a wine glass, hit a bronze key of a Balinese gamelan or drive a car over a speed bump. Each one rings at its own frequency. Almost every vibration problem in engineering starts from one model: a mass on a spring.

Equation of motion

A mass m sits on a spring of stiffness k. Measure x from the static equilibrium position, so gravity is already balanced by the spring’s preload and drops out. Displace the mass and the spring pushes back with −kx. Newton’s second law gives

mx¨+kx=0.

Try x=Acos(ωt)+Bsin(ωt). Substituting gives (k−mω2)x=0, so motion is possible only at

ωn​=mk​​,fn​=2πωn​​,T=2πkm​​.

A and B come from the start: A=x0​ and B=v0​/ωn​.

What the formula says

  • Stiffer means higher frequency; heavier means lower, both as square roots. Doubling the mass lengthens the period by 2​.
  • The frequency doesn’t depend on the amplitude. A linear spring gives the same period for small and large swings, which is why a tuning fork holds its pitch as it fades.
  • Energy swaps between the spring and the mass: 21​mx˙2+21​kx2 stays constant.

The static-deflection shortcut

Under gravity the spring sags by δ=mg/k. So k/m=g/δ and

fn​=2π1​δg​​.

Measure how much something sags and you know its natural frequency without weighing it. A sag of 25 mm gives about 3.2 Hz; 250 mm gives 1 Hz.

Worked exampleA quarter of a car

One corner of a car carries m=300 kg on a spring of k=30 kN/m (ignore the damper for now).

  1. ωn​=30000/300​=10.000 rad/s, so fn​=1.5915 Hz and T=0.6283 s.
  2. Simulating 10 s with velocity Verlet at Δt=1 ms and measuring zero crossings gives 0.628316 s against 2πm/k​=0.628319 s.
  3. Released from 50 mm the energy is 37.5 J, conserved to 2.5×10−5. Releasing from 1 mm or 200 mm gives the same period.
  4. Static sag 300⋅9.81/30000=98.1 mm, and 9.81/0.0981​/2π=1.5915 Hz, the same answer.
  5. Doubling the mass to 600 kg gives a period of 0.8886 s, a ratio of 1.4142.

Car suspensions are tuned to about 1 to 1.5 Hz, close to the rhythm of walking, which people find comfortable.

Exercise 1A gamelan key

A bronze gamelan key rings at 440 Hz. Treat its first mode as a mass-spring with an effective mass of 0.12 kg. What effective stiffness does that imply? If the maker grinds the key so its effective mass drops by 4 % with the same stiffness, what is the new pitch?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. k=mωn2​=0.12⋅(2π⋅440)2=9.17×105 N/m.
  2. f∝1/m​, so f=440/0.96​=449.1 Hz.
  3. Real tuning is subtler: grinding the middle of a bar reduces its stiffness more than its mass and lowers the pitch, while grinding the ends raises it.

quiz.q: Natural frequency (Hz) of 300 kg on a 30 kN/m spring. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: fn​=k/m​/2π.

quiz.q: Natural frequency (Hz) of a machine that sags 25 mm on its mounts. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: fn​=g/δ​/2π.

quiz.q: Effective stiffness (N/m) of the 440 Hz key with 0.12 kg effective mass. 3 significant figures.
quiz.explain: k=mωn2​.

quiz.q: Doubling the amplitude of a linear oscillator changes its period by…
quiz.explain: The period is independent of amplitude.

quiz.q: To halve a natural frequency at fixed mass you must…
quiz.explain: f∝k​.

08.02.title: Damping
08.02.html:
A real oscillator dies away. Friction in joints, air drag, internal friction in rubber and steel, and purpose-built shock absorbers all turn vibration energy into heat. The simplest model that captures this, and the one engineers use almost everywhere, is a viscous damper: a force proportional to velocity.

The damped equation

Add a damper of coefficient c (N s/m):

mx¨+cx˙+kx=0.

Divide by m and write it with two numbers that describe any such system, the natural frequency ωn​=k/m​ and the damping ratio

ζ=2km​c​,x¨+2ζωn​x˙+ωn2​x=0.

Trying x=est gives s=−ζωn​±ωn​ζ2−1​. Three cases follow.

  • Underdamped, ζ<1: it oscillates at the damped frequency ωd​=ωn​1−ζ2​ inside an envelope e−ζωn​t. Almost all structures and machines are here, typically with ζ from 0.005 (a steel bridge) to 0.3 (a car suspension).
  • Critically damped, ζ=1: the fastest return to rest without overshoot. Door closers and gauge needles aim for this.
  • Overdamped, ζ>1: no oscillation, and a slower creep back.

Logarithmic decrement

You can’t easily measure c directly, but you can record a decaying vibration. Successive peaks one damped period apart shrink by a constant factor. The logarithmic decrement is

δ=lnxi+1​xi​​=1−ζ2​2πζ​,ζ=4π2+δ2​δ​.

For light damping, measure over n cycles and use δ=n1​ln(xi​/xi+n​). With noisy data, fitting a straight line through lnxi​ against cycle number uses every peak and is better still.

Worked exampleFinding ζ from a recording

Quarter-car: m=300 kg, k=30 kN/m, damper c=1200 N s/m, released from 50 mm.

  1. ζ=1200/(230000⋅300​)=0.200; ωd​=101−0.04​=9.798 rad/s.
  2. Simulated peaks (refined with a parabola through three samples): 13.87, 3.85, 1.07, 0.30 mm. Each is 0.2773 times the previous.
  3. δ=ln(1/0.2773)=1.2825, so ζ=1.2825/4π2+1.28252​=0.2000. The test asked for 2 %; it hits it exactly.
  4. A lightly damped structure with ζ=0.01: both one-cycle and ten-cycle estimates give 0.01000 from clean data. Add 0.5 mm of random noise and the one-cycle estimate drifts to 0.0098, while a straight-line fit over 29 cycles still returns 0.0100.

Exercise 1A footbridge test

Engineers jump on a footbridge and record its decay. The peak acceleration falls from 0.80 m/s² to 0.35 m/s² over 12 cycles at 2.1 Hz. Estimate ζ. How long does it take to fall to 5 % of its starting level?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. δ=121​ln(0.80/0.35)=0.06889.
  2. ζ=0.06889/4π2+0.068892​=0.01096, about 1.1 %, typical of a steel footbridge.
  3. The amplitude falls by e−δ per cycle: n=ln20/δ=43.5 cycles, which is 20.7 s at 2.1 Hz.

quiz.q: Damping ratio of m = 300 kg, k = 30 kN/m, c = 1200 N s/m. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: c/(2km​).

quiz.q: Log decrement for ζ = 0.05. 5 decimals.
quiz.explain: 2πζ/1−ζ2​.

quiz.q: Damping ratio of the footbridge (0.80 to 0.35 m/s² in 12 cycles). 5 decimals.
quiz.explain: δ=n1​ln(x0​/xn​).

quiz.q: A door closer should be…
quiz.explain: Fastest return without slamming past.

quiz.q: For light damping, why measure the decrement over many cycles?
quiz.explain: Many cycles give a large, well-measured ratio.
options: The amplitude change per cycle is tiny, so noise dominates a one-cycle ratio

08.03.title: Forced vibration and resonance
08.03.html:
Push a child on a swing at the right moment and small pushes build a big swing. Machines do the same to whatever they sit on: an unbalanced pump on a floor, an engine in a car body, a crowd on a grandstand. When the forcing frequency nears a natural frequency, the response can be many times larger than the static deflection. That’s resonance.

Steady-state response

Drive the damped oscillator with a harmonic force F0​cosωt:

mx¨+cx˙+kx=F0​cosωt.

After the start-up transient decays, the mass moves at the forcing frequency with amplitude X and a phase lag φ. Using complex notation, F=F0​eiωt and x=Xei(ωt−φ), the frequency response (receptance) is

H(ω)=F0​Xe−iφ​=k−mω2+icω1​.

With the frequency ratio r=ω/ωn​:

F0​/kX​=(1−r2)2+(2ζr)2​1​,tanφ=1−r22ζr​.

Three regions

  • Well below resonance (r≪1): the spring dominates. X≈F0​/k, in phase with the force.
  • At resonance (r=1): spring and inertia cancel and only damping limits the motion. X=(F0​/k)/(2ζ), lagging the force by 90°. That 90° lag is the cleanest way to spot a resonance in a test.
  • Well above resonance (r≫1): inertia dominates. X≈F0​/(mω2), falling fast, and 180° out of phase.

The amplitude peaks slightly below ωn​, at ωn​1−2ζ2​, with height 1/(2ζ1−ζ2​). For ζ>0.707 there is no peak at all.

Worked exampleA machine on rubber mounts

m=200 kg, k=2×105 N/m, ζ=0.05, driven by F0​=500 N.

  1. ωn​=31.623 rad/s (5.033 Hz); c=2ζkm​=632.5 N s/m; static deflection F0​/k=2.50 mm.
  2. Searching ∣H∣ on a fine grid puts the peak at 31.544 rad/s, matching ωn​1−2ζ2​=31.544.
  3. Peak amplitude 25.031 mm, an amplification of 10.0125, matching 1/(2ζ1−ζ2​).
  4. Integrating the forced equation for 60 cycles with RK4 and measuring the last 5:
r ∣H∣F0​ (mm) simulated (mm) phase lag
0.5 3.3260 3.3259 3.81°
1.0 25.0000 25.0000 90.00°
2.0 0.8315 0.8315 176.19°

Exercise 1Staying clear of resonance

A 50 kg fan unit on springs with ζ=0.03 runs at 1450 rpm. Its rotor produces a 40 N force at running speed. The springs give a natural frequency of 20 Hz. Find the amplitude at running speed, and what it would be if the springs were swapped for ones giving 24 Hz.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ω=1450⋅2π/60=151.8 rad/s, which is 24.17 Hz.
  2. With fn​=20 Hz: k=50(2π⋅20)2=7.896×105 N/m, r=1.208, amplification 1/(1−1.460)2+(0.0725)2​=2.147. X=2.147⋅40/7.896×105=0.109 mm.
  3. With fn​=24 Hz: r=1.007, amplification 16.1, and X=0.57 mm, five times worse. Stiffer is not always better; here softer springs (lower fn​) would help most.

quiz.q: Dynamic amplification at resonance (r = 1) for ζ = 0.05.
quiz.explain: 1/(2ζ).

quiz.q: Peak frequency (rad/s) for ω_n = 31.623 rad/s and ζ = 0.05. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: ωn​1−2ζ2​.

quiz.q: Fan amplitude (mm) with the 20 Hz springs. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: Amplification 2.15 on 0.0507 mm static.

quiz.q: At resonance the displacement lags the force by…
quiz.explain: tanφ→∞.

quiz.q: Far above resonance the amplitude is controlled mainly by…
quiz.explain: X≈F0​/(mω2).

08.04.title: Base excitation and isolation
08.04.html:
Often the force doesn’t act on the mass. Instead the ground moves: a bike wheel rolling over cobbles, a car on a rough road, a laboratory microscope on a floor shaken by traffic. The spring and damper carry that motion up to the mass. Choose them well and most of the shaking never arrives. That’s vibration isolation.

Equation of motion

The base moves as y(t) and the mass as x(t). The spring and damper respond to the relative motion:

mx¨+c(x˙−y˙​)+k(x−y)=0.

For y=Ysinωt the mass moves at the same frequency with amplitude X. The transmissibility is

T=YX​=(1−r2)2+(2ζr)21+(2ζr)2​​,r=ωn​ω​.

The same formula gives the force passed into the ground by a vibrating machine on mounts, FT​/F0​. So isolating a sensitive instrument from the floor, and the floor from a noisy machine, are the same problem.

The √2 rule

Set T=1 and solve: r=2​, whatever the damping. Below 2​ωn​ the mount amplifies the motion; above it, it isolates. So an isolator must be soft: its natural frequency well below the disturbing frequency, ideally r≥3.

Damping cuts both ways. It limits the peak at resonance (which every machine passes through as it starts) but makes isolation worse above 2​, because the damper itself pushes the mass along with the base.

Worked exampleA mountain bike on cobbles

Rider and frame m=80 kg on a suspension of k=25 kN/m with ζ=0.3. Cobbles 0.25 m apart, 10 mm from peak to trough (Y=5 mm).

  1. fn​=25000/80​/2π=2.813 Hz; c=849 N s/m.
  2. At 2 m/s the cobbles come at 8 Hz, r=2.843: T=0.2714. Simulating 6 s with RK4 gives 0.2714. At 5 m/s (20 Hz, r=7.109): T=0.0881, simulated 0.0881.
  3. Damping trade-off. At resonance T = 5.10, 1.94 and 1.30 for ζ = 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6. At r=3: 0.145, 0.251 and 0.426.
  4. A single 30 mm half-sine bump 0.3 m long: the rider rises 39.8 mm at 1 m/s (slow bump, overshoot), 25.3 mm at 3 m/s and only 10.2 mm at 8 m/s. Fast riding over sharp bumps is smoother.

Exercise 1Isolating a compressor

A 120 kg compressor runs at 1800 rpm. You want only 10 % of its shaking force to reach the floor. Ignoring damping, what natural frequency, and so what total mount stiffness, do you need? How much will the mounts sag?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. With ζ=0, T=1/(r2−1)=0.1, so r2=11 and r=3.317.
  2. Running frequency 30 Hz, so fn​=30/3.317=9.045 Hz.
  3. k=m(2πfn​)2=120⋅(56.83)2=3.876×105 N/m in total.
  4. Static sag mg/k=3.04 mm. Isolators are often chosen straight from a sag chart for this reason.

quiz.q: Transmissibility at r = 2.843 with ζ = 0.3. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: The base-excitation formula.

quiz.q: Required mount stiffness (kN/m) for the compressor. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: r=11​.

quiz.q: Transmissibility exactly at r = √2 with ζ = 0.4.
quiz.explain: The crossover is independent of damping.

quiz.q: To isolate a sensitive instrument from floor vibration you want mounts that are…
quiz.explain: Isolation needs r>2​, ideally 3 or more.
options: Soft, with natural frequency well below the disturbance

quiz.q: Above r=2​, adding damping…
quiz.explain: The damper drags the mass along with the base.

08.05.title: Rotating unbalance
08.05.html:
A washing machine on spin walks across the floor; a fan with a bent blade rattles its housing; a turbine with a lost blade fragment shakes its bearings. Each has a rotating part whose centre of mass is not on the axis. That small offset creates a force that grows with the square of speed.

The forcing

An unbalanced mass m at eccentricity e spins at ω inside a machine of total mass M (including m), mounted on a spring k and damper c. The lump needs a centripetal force meω2, so it pulls the machine with a rotating force of that size. Its vertical component drives the vertical motion:

Mx¨+cx˙+kx=meω2cosωt.

This is forced vibration with F0​=meω2, so the amplitude is

meMX​=(1−r2)2+(2ζr)2​r2​.

Three regions again

  • Low speed: the force meω2 is small, and so is X, growing as r2.
  • Resonance: X=Mme​⋅2ζ1​. The machine must pass through quickly, and the damping must be enough to keep this tolerable.
  • High speed: X→me/M. The rotor and machine now spin about their combined centre of mass, which stays still. The amplitude stops growing however fast it spins. That’s why a washing machine is noisy as it spins up and calmer at full speed.

The force into the floor is the transmissibility times meω2. It keeps growing with speed above 2​ωn​, but much more slowly than the unbalance force itself.

Worked exampleA washing machine

Drum assembly M=40 kg, a 0.5 kg lump of wet laundry at e=0.25 m, suspension k=40 kN/m, ζ=0.1.

  1. Resonance at ωn​=31.62 rad/s, which is 302 rpm. me/M=3.125 mm.
  2. Steady amplitudes, checked by an 80-cycle RK4 simulation where shown:
speed amplitude simulated force to floor lump’s pull meω2
150 rpm 1.015 mm 1.015 41 N 31 N
302 rpm 15.626 mm 637 N 125 N
600 rpm 4.148 mm 4.147 179 N 493 N
1400 rpm 3.274 mm 3.274 179 N 2687 N
  1. At resonance the floor feels five times the unbalance force. At 1400 rpm it feels only 7 % of it, while the drum moves about me/M. (That 600 and 1400 rpm give the same floor force here is a coincidence of ζ=0.1.)
  2. At very high speed the amplitude is 3.1250 mm, exactly me/M.

Exercise 1A pump on a frame

A 250 kg pump has a rotor unbalance of me=0.002 kg m. It sits on a frame with fn​=12 Hz and ζ=0.05. Find the amplitude at its running speed of 2900 rpm, and at resonance during start-up.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. me/M=0.002/250=8.0×10−6 m.
  2. Running: r=(2900/60)/12=4.028. r2=16.22, and r2/(1−16.22)2+(0.4028)2​=1.0653. X=8.52 μm.
  3. Resonance: X=8 μm/(2⋅0.05)=80 μm, ten times the steady running value.

quiz.q: High-speed amplitude limit (mm) for M = 40 kg, m = 0.5 kg, e = 0.25 m. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: me/M.

quiz.q: Amplitude (μm) of the pump at 2900 rpm. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Mme​r2/(1−r2)2+(2ζr)2​.

quiz.q: Centripetal pull (N) of 0.5 kg at 0.25 m at 1400 rpm. Nearest newton.
quiz.explain: meω2.

quiz.q: Why does the drum amplitude stop growing at high speed?
quiz.explain: X→me/M.
options: The drum and lump spin about their combined centre of mass, which stays still

quiz.q: At resonance the amplitude of an unbalanced rotor on mounts is…
quiz.explain: Set r=1.
options: me/M
Mme​2ζ1​

08.06.title: Two-DOF systems
08.06.html:
Hang two pendulums side by side and join them with a weak spring. Start one swinging and leave the other still. Slowly the first one stops and the second takes over, then they swap back. Nothing is lost; the energy just passes between them. Explaining that needs the idea at the centre of all structural dynamics: modes.

Equations in matrix form

A system with two coordinates x=(x1​,x2​) obeys

Mx¨+Kx=0,

with a symmetric mass matrix M and stiffness matrix K. For the chain wall, spring k1​, mass m1​, spring k2​, mass m2​:

M=[m1​0​0m2​​],K=[k1​+k2​−k2​​−k2​k2​​].

Modes as an eigenproblem

Look for motions where every coordinate moves in step at one frequency: x=ϕcosωt. Substituting gives

(K−ω2M)ϕ=0.

A non-zero ϕ needs det(K−ω2M)=0, a quadratic in ω2 with two roots: two natural frequencies, each with its mode shape ϕi​. Any free motion is a mix of the two modes.

Orthogonality

The mode shapes are not perpendicular in the ordinary sense, but they are M-orthogonal and K-orthogonal:

ϕ1T​Mϕ2​=0,ϕ1T​Kϕ2​=0.

Scaling each so that ϕiT​Mϕi​=1 (mass normalisation) makes ΦTMΦ=I and ΦTKΦ=diag(ωi2​). This is what lets 08.08 split big systems into independent oscillators.

Beats

For the coupled pendulums the modes are obvious: swinging together at ω1​=g/l​ (the spring never stretches), and swinging opposite at ω2​=g/l+2k/m​. Pulling one pendulum aside starts both modes with equal amplitude. Their sum is

θ1​=2θ0​​(cosω1​t+cosω2​t)=θ0​cos2ω2​−ω1​​tcos2ω2​+ω1​​t,

a fast swing inside a slow envelope. The energy moves to the other pendulum and back once every beat period 2π/(ω2​−ω1​). Two gamelan instruments tuned slightly apart beat in exactly this way, and Balinese tuning uses it on purpose to make the sound shimmer.

Worked exampleCoupled pendulums and a two-mass chain

  1. Pendulums: m=1 kg, l=1 m, coupling spring 0.5 N/m between the bobs. Solving the eigenproblem gives 3.1321 rad/s with shape (1, 1) and 3.2879 rad/s with shape (1, −1), matching g/l​ and g/l+2k/m​ to machine precision.
  2. Mass-normalised: ΦTMΦ=I, and ΦTKΦ has 9.81 and 10.81 on its diagonal, the squared frequencies.
  3. Start pendulum 1 at 0.1 rad. Beat period 40.34 s. Half a beat later, at 20.17 s, pendulum 2 swings with the full 0.1000 rad and pendulum 1 is almost still.
  4. Chain m1​=2, m2​=1 kg, k1​=2000, k2​=1000 N/m: frequencies 22.3607 and 44.7214 rad/s with shapes (1, 2) and (1, −1). Their plain dot product is −0.2357 after mass-normalising, but with M in between it is −8×10−17, zero to rounding.

Exercise 1Modes by hand

For the chain m1​=2 kg, m2​=1 kg, k1​=2000 N/m, k2​=1000 N/m, write det(K−ω2M)=0 and solve it.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. K=[3000−1000​−10001000​]. With λ=ω2: (3000−2λ)(1000−λ)−106=0.
  2. Expand: 2λ2−5000λ+2×106=0, so λ=500 or 2000.
  3. ω1​=22.36 rad/s, ω2​=44.72 rad/s.
  4. Mode 1 from the second row: −1000ϕ1​+(1000−500)ϕ2​=0, so ϕ2​=2ϕ1​. Mode 2: ϕ2​=−ϕ1​.

quiz.q: Beat period (s) of two 1 m pendulums with a 0.5 N/m coupling spring and 1 kg bobs. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: 2π/(ω2​−ω1​).

quiz.q: Higher natural frequency (rad/s) of the 2 kg / 1 kg chain. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: λ=2000.

quiz.q: For mode shapes (1, 2) and (1, −1) with M = diag(2, 1), compute ϕ1T​Mϕ2​.
quiz.explain: 2⋅1⋅1+1⋅2⋅(−1)=0.

quiz.q: Mode shapes of a system with unequal masses are generally…
quiz.explain: M-orthogonality.
options: Orthogonal with respect to M and K

quiz.q: If you start the coupled pendulums swinging together in phase…
quiz.explain: Only mode 1 is excited.
options: They stay in phase for ever (one mode only)

08.07.title: Tuned mass dampers
08.07.html:
On its opening day in 2000, London’s Millennium Bridge began to sway sideways under the crowd and was closed two days later. The fix included dozens of tuned mass dampers. Taipei 101 has a 660 t steel ball hanging near its top for the same reason. A tuned mass damper (TMD) is a small oscillator attached to a big one, tuned so that it absorbs the big one’s resonance.

How it works

Attach a mass m2​ on a spring k2​ and damper c2​ to the structure’s modal mass m1​. Near the structure’s natural frequency the TMD swings strongly and out of phase. Its spring then pushes back on the structure, cancelling much of the forcing, and its damper turns that motion into heat. The pair is a two-DOF system (08.06) with two resonances instead of one tall one.

With the mass ratio μ=m2​/m1​, tuning ratio f=ω2​/ω1​ and TMD damping ζ2​, the structure’s response comes from the 2×2 complex system

[k1​+k2​−m1​ω2+iω(c1​+c2​)−k2​−iωc2​​−k2​−iωc2​k2​−m2​ω2+iωc2​​][X1​X2​​]=[F0​0​].

Den Hartog’s tuning

For an undamped structure, J. P. Den Hartog found in 1934 that every response curve passes through two fixed points, whatever the TMD damping. The best design makes them equal in height and puts the peaks on them:

fopt​=1+μ1​,ζ2,opt​=8(1+μ)33μ​​,(F0​/k1​X1​​)max​≈1+μ2​​.

A heavier TMD works better and is less sensitive to mistuning, but it costs space and money. Typical mass ratios are 1 to 5 %.

Worked exampleA footbridge TMD

First vertical mode at 2.0 Hz (walking pace), modal mass 50 t, structural damping ζ1​=0.5 %.

  1. Without a TMD the peak amplification is 1/(2ζ1​)=100.
  2. μ=0.02, a 1000 kg TMD. Den Hartog: tuned to 2.0/1.02=1.9608 Hz with ζ2​=0.0841. The peak drops to 9.34 (the undamped-bridge formula gives 10.05).
  3. SciPy’s Nelder-Mead, minimising the peak directly with the bridge’s own damping included, finds f=0.9794, ζ2​=0.0866 and a peak of 9.25. Den Hartog is within 1 %.
  4. If the bridge turns out to be at 2.10 Hz instead of 2.00 Hz, the same TMD gives a peak of 14.22. A TMD tuned to three times the bridge frequency does nothing: 99.62.
  5. Mass ratio 1 % gives a peak of 12.74; 5 % gives 6.14.

Exercise 1Sizing a TMD

A floor has a 1.5 Hz mode with a modal mass of 30 t. You want a peak amplification of no more than about 12. What mass ratio, TMD mass, tuned frequency and TMD damping does Den Hartog suggest?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. 1+2/μ​=12 gives 2/μ=143, so μ=0.01399, about 1.4 %.
  2. TMD mass 0.01399⋅30000=420 kg.
  3. Tuning 1.5/1.01399=1.479 Hz.
  4. ζ2​=3⋅0.01399/(8⋅1.013993)​=0.0709.

quiz.q: Den Hartog optimal TMD damping for μ = 0.02. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: 3μ/(8(1+μ)3)​.

quiz.q: Optimal TMD frequency (Hz) for a 2.0 Hz bridge with μ = 0.02. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: fopt​=1/(1+μ).

quiz.q: Approximate peak amplification with a Den Hartog TMD of μ = 0.05. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: 1+2/μ​=41​.

quiz.q: A TMD with too little damping…
quiz.explain: Two lightly damped modes remain.
options: Splits the resonance into two tall peaks

quiz.q: Why are TMDs sensitive to mistuning?
quiz.explain: A 5 % frequency error raised the peak from 9.3 to 14.2.
options: They work only near the frequency they are tuned to

08.08.title: Multi-DOF systems and modal analysis
08.08.html:
A building in an earthquake, a car body on its suspension, an aircraft wing: their models have hundreds to millions of coupled coordinates. Solving them directly is possible but costly and hard to interpret. Modal analysis turns one big coupled problem into many independent single oscillators, of which usually only a handful matter.

Modal coordinates

For Mx¨+Cx˙+Kx=F(t) with n coordinates, solve the eigenproblem (K−ω2M)ϕ=0 for n frequencies and mass-normalised mode shapes, collected as columns of Φ. Write the motion as a mix of modes:

x(t)=Φq(t)=i∑​ϕi​qi​(t).

Substitute and multiply by ΦT. Orthogonality (08.06) makes the mass and stiffness matrices diagonal. If the damping is also diagonal in modal coordinates (assumed by giving each mode a damping ratio ζi​), every mode decouples:

q¨​i​+2ζi​ωi​q˙​i​+ωi2​qi​=ϕiT​F(t).

Each is the single oscillator of 08.02 and 08.03. Solve them separately and add them back up: modal superposition.

Ground shaking

For a building whose base accelerates at ag​(t), the effective force is F=−M1ag​. Mode i is driven by Li​=ϕiT​M1, its participation factor. The effective modal mass Li2​ tells how much of the building’s mass the mode moves. Building codes require enough modes to reach 90 % of the total. For regular buildings the first mode alone often carries 80 % or more, which is why simple hand methods work.

Worked exampleA five-storey frame in an earthquake pulse

Floors of 20 t, storey stiffness 40 MN/m, 2 % damping in every mode. Ground acceleration 2sin(2π⋅1.5t) m/s² for 4 s.

  1. scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M) gives 2.0259, 5.9135, 9.3221, 11.9755 and 13.6586 Hz. Mode 1 shape, roof = 1: 0.2846, 0.5462, 0.7635, 0.9190, 1.
  2. Effective modal masses: 87.95, 8.72, 2.42, 0.75 and 0.16 % of the total. Two modes pass 90 %.
  3. Integrating all ten coupled first-order equations directly with RK4 (Δt=2 ms, 10 s) and integrating five separate modal oscillators give the same displacements to a relative difference of 1.1×10−14.
  4. Peak roof displacement 53.261 mm. Mode 1 alone gives 53.709 mm, within 1 %. Peak base shear 635.8 kN.

Exercise 1A two-storey check

A two-storey shear building has floor masses m and storey stiffnesses k, so M=mI and K=k[2−1​−11​]. Find both frequencies in terms of k/m​, and the first mode’s effective modal mass as a fraction of the total.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. det(K−λM)=0: (2k−λm)(k−λm)−k2=0, so λ=23∓5​​k/m.
  2. ω1​=0.618k/m​, ω2​=1.618k/m​ (the golden ratio appears).
  3. Mode 1 from row 2: −kϕ1​+(k−0.382k)ϕ2​=0, so ϕ=(0.618,1).
  4. L=m(0.618+1)=1.618m; ϕTMϕ=m(0.382+1)=1.382m. Effective mass L2/(ϕTMϕ)=1.894m, which is 94.7 % of 2m.

quiz.q: First frequency of the 2-storey building as a multiple of √(k/m). 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: λ1​=(3−5​)/2.

quiz.q: Effective modal mass of mode 1 of that building, % of total. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: L2/(ϕTMϕ) over 2m.

quiz.q: How many modes does a model with 5 degrees of freedom have?
quiz.explain: One per degree of freedom.

quiz.q: Modal superposition requires…
quiz.explain: Otherwise the modes stay coupled.
options: A linear system with damping that is diagonal in modal coordinates

quiz.q: Effective modal mass tells you…
quiz.explain: Li2​ with mass-normalised modes.
options: How much of the structure’s mass a mode moves under ground shaking

08.09.title: Vibration of strings
08.09.html:
A string has infinitely many degrees of freedom: every point along it can move. Yet a guitar string still has distinct modes, and their frequencies come out as exact whole-number multiples of the lowest. That’s why a string sounds like a clear musical note, while a drum or a bell sounds more clangorous.

The wave equation

Take a string of tension T and mass per length μ. A small element dx that is curved feels a net vertical force from the tension at its two ends, T∂2y/∂x2dx. Newton’s law for the element gives

μ∂t2∂2y​=T∂x2∂2y​,c=μT​​.

Here c is the speed at which waves travel along the string.

Standing waves

With both ends fixed, look for solutions y=sin(nπx/L)cos(ωn​t). Each satisfies the end conditions, and the wave equation then requires ωn​=nπc/L:

fn​=2Lnc​=2Ln​μT​​,n=1,2,3,…

The modes are harmonics: f,2f,3f,…. Mode n has n−1 nodes, points that never move. Musicians use this: lightly touching a string at its midpoint kills every odd mode and leaves the octave.

Plucking

The pluck shape sets how much of each mode is present. A string pulled aside by h at position xp​ and released is a triangle. Its sine-series coefficients are

bn​=n2π2xp​(L−xp​)2hL2​sinLnπxp​​.

They fall as 1/n2. Any mode with a node at the pluck point is missing: pluck at L/5 and harmonics 5, 10, 15 are silent. Plucking near the bridge excites more high harmonics and sounds brighter.

Worked exampleA guitar’s high E string

Scale length L=0.65 m, tension 70 N, tuned to f1​=329.63 Hz.

  1. c=2Lf1​=428.5 m/s, so μ=T/c2=0.3812 g/m. The whole string weighs 0.248 g.
  2. Plucked 3 mm at L/5: modal amplitudes 2.2333, 0.9034, 0.4015, 0.1396, 0 mm, then −0.0620, … with harmonic 10 also exactly 0.
  3. Checking against a finite-difference simulation of the wave equation (500 cells, leapfrog at Courant number 1): at 0.1 m from the end over 0.05 s, the two agree to within 3.5 µm on a 3 mm pluck.
  4. One second of synthesised sound at 44.1 kHz with a little decay: spectral peaks at 329.62, 659.27, 988.88, 1318.52, then 1977.77 Hz. The ratios are 1, 2.0001, 3.0001, 4.0002, 6.0002: whole numbers, with 5 missing.

Exercise 1Restringing

A bass guitar’s open E string (f1​=41.2 Hz) has a scale length of 0.864 m and a mass of 18 g/m. What tension does it need? If you tune it down a whole tone to D (36.7 Hz), by how much does the tension fall?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. c=2Lf1​=2⋅0.864⋅41.2=71.19 m/s.
  2. T=μc2=0.018⋅71.192=91.2 N.
  3. Tension scales with f2: (36.7/41.2)2=0.7935, so T=72.4 N, about 21 % less.

quiz.q: Tension (N) for the bass E string. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: T=μ(2Lf)2.

quiz.q: Fundamental (Hz) of a 0.65 m string with T = 70 N and μ = 0.3812 g/m. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: f1​=T/μ​/2L.

quiz.q: A string plucked at L/4: what is the lowest missing harmonic?
quiz.explain: sin(nπ/4)=0 first at n=4.

quiz.q: Quadrupling the tension of a string changes its pitch by…
quiz.explain: f∝T​.

quiz.q: Why do strings sound like clear notes?
quiz.explain: Harmonic overtones.
options: Their mode frequencies are whole-number multiples of the fundamental
